hook: You know Philippians 4:13. But did you know Paul wrote it about going hungry and having plenty, while he was a prisoner?
story:
Paul knew Philippi from the inside of its jail.

On his first visit he and Silas were dragged before the magistrates, stripped and “beaten with rods”. After many blows they were locked in the inner cell with their feet in the stocks. Then comes one of the most remarkable sentences in the book of Acts: “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.”

Before morning the jailer himself had washed their wounds and been baptized.

Years later Paul writes to the church that grew out of that night. He is a prisoner again. He tells them he has learned to be content, full or hungry, in plenty or in need. So when the believers in Philippi first read “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me”, they were reading the words of a man who had sung in their own prison.
moment:
Paul is writing from custody. Earlier in the letter he mentions “my bonds”, and says the whole palace guard has come to know why he is held.

He is writing to friends. The church in Philippi had cared for him before, and now, after a time when they could not, they have sent help again. It moves him: “I rejoice in the Lord greatly that now at length you have revived your thought for me”. This famous sentence stands in a thank-you letter. He wants them to know two things at once: that their gift mattered to him, and that he would have been at peace without it.
around: The two verses before it say what the “all things” are: “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it”, and “both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need”.
readings:
Today many people carry this verse into a contest, an exam or an operating room, and they have drawn real courage from it.

Others have pushed back, sometimes sharply, and said the verse has nothing to do with winning. Paul is speaking of contentment, in hunger as well as in plenty.

There is truth on both sides. The verse is about strength, and Paul means the strength to stay faithful and at peace whatever happens. That includes the hard thing in front of a person. It also includes losing.
argued:
For years the quarterback Tim Tebow wore this verse on his eye black, until such messages were banned in 2010. Speaking in 2012 about why he had chosen it, he said [[tebow]] The basketball player Stephen Curry has written a version of it on his shoes since his college days, as a 2019 fact check by PolitiFact confirmed.

In the sixteenth century John Calvin had already drawn a line around the words all things. In his commentary on this letter he wrote: [[calvin]] The pastor John Piper reads it the same way today: in Paul’s letter, all things includes going hungry, suffering and being in want.

So the verse lives in two places at once: on the field before a game, and in the cell of a prisoner who had learned to be content with little. Both ask it for strength. They differ on what the strength is for.
point: The strength Paul speaks of is strength to be content, in hunger as much as in plenty. The verse is about enduring any circumstance with Christ, more than about winning in every one.
